lisbon.name: Lisbon
facts: Old yellow trams climb Lisbon’s steep, narrow streets. Tram 28 rattles through the oldest neighbourhoods of the city.
Lisbon is called the city of seven hills. The Santa Justa Lift, an iron tower more than 100 years old, carries people up one of them.
Try a pastel de nata, a little custard tart with a crispy crust. In Belém they have baked them to a secret recipe since 1837.
Many houses are covered with azulejos: shiny painted tiles, often blue and white. Lisbon even has a whole museum of tiles.
The Oceanário is one of the biggest aquariums in Europe. Sea otters, sharks and rays live there.
The Vasco da Gama Bridge over the river Tagus is more than 12 kilometres long. It is one of the longest bridges in Europe.

events.d: In late spring the jacaranda trees cover themselves in purple flowers, and whole streets turn lilac.
In June the streets fill with garlands, grilled sardines and singing parades, and friends give each other little pots of basil.
In summer families head to the beaches of Cascais and Caparica. The Atlantic is chilly, but the waves are fun.
In autumn smoky street carts sell hot roasted chestnuts, and on 11 November, St Martin’s Day, everybody eats them.
The streets glow with lights, and families share bolo-rei, a ring-shaped cake with candied fruit that looks like a crown.

tf.s: Lisbon’s famous old trams are yellow.
tf.w: The old yellow trams go up and down the steep hills.

tf.s: Many houses in Lisbon are decorated with painted tiles.
tf.w: The tiles are called azulejos, and many are blue and white.

tf.s: Lisbon stands on the shore of the Mediterranean Sea.
tf.w: Lisbon stands on the river Tagus, right next to the Atlantic Ocean.

tf.s: A pastel de nata is filled with chocolate.
tf.w: It is filled with sweet egg custard and is often sprinkled with cinnamon.

porto.name: Porto
facts: The Dom Luís I Bridge has two levels: metro trains cross on top, high above the river, and cars drive across below.
Climb the narrow stairs of the Clérigos Tower, a tall old bell tower, to see the whole city from the top.
The hall of São Bento railway station is decorated with about 20,000 blue-and-white tiles. Their pictures tell stories from the past.
Livraria Lello is one of the most beautiful bookshops in the world. Inside, a curving red staircase seems to float.
In the gardens of the Crystal Palace, peacocks stroll freely among the trees and flowers.
Porto’s famous sandwich is the francesinha. It is huge, and it is covered with melted cheese and a special sauce.

events.d: At the end of winter, red, pink and white camellias bloom in Porto’s old gardens.
On the night of 23 June people playfully tap each other on the head with squeaky plastic hammers. Then fireworks light up the river.
In summer people go to the ocean beaches where the river Douro meets the Atlantic. The water is very fresh!
In September grapes are picked in the Douro Valley, where the hillsides look like giant steps covered with vines.
In December the city centre sparkles with lights, and a big Christmas tree stands on the main avenue.

tf.s: The Dom Luís I Bridge in Porto has two levels, one above the other.
tf.w: Metro trains cross on the top level and cars on the lower one.

tf.s: On St John’s Night people tap each other on the head with plastic hammers.
tf.w: It is a friendly joke: the soft hammers squeak and everybody laughs.

tf.s: Porto is the capital of Portugal.
tf.w: The capital is Lisbon. Porto is the second biggest city in Portugal.

tf.s: Kangaroos hop around freely in the Crystal Palace gardens in Porto.
tf.w: It is peacocks that stroll there freely. There are no kangaroos.

algarve.name: Algarve
facts: The Algarve is the sunny south of Portugal, with golden cliffs, sea caves and rocks shaped like arches.
Benagil Cave is a sea cave with a round hole in its roof, like a window to the sky. You can see it from a boat.
Seahorses live in the Ria Formosa lagoon, and pink flamingos often wade in its shallow water.
Boat trips go out to sea to watch dolphins jumping and playing in the waves.
Look at the roofs: Algarve houses have white chimneys with lacy patterns. People say no two are alike.
Try the little almond sweets shaped like fruits and animals. They are made of almonds and sugar, a treat of the Algarve.

events.d: In winter the almond trees turn white with flowers. A legend says a king planted them so his princess from the north could see ‘snow’.
The town of Loulé holds one of the oldest carnivals in Portugal, with colourful floats, costumes and music.
In spring white storks raise their chicks in huge nests on towers, poles and tall chimneys.
In summer the sea on the Algarve’s south coast is warmer than on Portugal’s west coast. Time to swim and build sandcastles!
In autumn thousands of birds, such as storks, eagles and kites, fly over Sagres on their way to Africa.

tf.s: The south-western corner of mainland Europe is in the Algarve.
tf.w: It is Cape St Vincent, a windy cape with a lighthouse.

tf.s: Seahorses live in the Ria Formosa lagoon.
tf.w: The seahorses hide among the underwater grass there.

tf.s: It snows in the Algarve every winter.
tf.w: It almost never snows there. But in winter the white almond blossom looks like snow.

tf.s: The Algarve is in the north of Portugal.
tf.w: It is the very south of Portugal, by the sea.

madeira.name: Madeira
facts: Madeira is an island in the Atlantic Ocean, the top of an old volcano. It is closer to Africa than to Lisbon.
It is called the island of eternal spring: it is mild all year, and flowers bloom everywhere, like the orange bird-of-paradise flower.
In Monte you can ride downhill in a wicker sledge on wooden runners. Two men dressed in white, with straw hats, steer it.
Paths run beside the levadas, old water channels, through an ancient laurel forest protected by UNESCO.
Try bolo do caco, a round flatbread baked on a hot stone and spread with garlic butter.
The famous footballer Cristiano Ronaldo was born in Madeira, and the island’s airport is named after him.

events.d: A parade full of music, sequins and feathers dances through Funchal, the island’s capital, with everyone in bright costumes.
In spring children bring flowers to build a ‘Wall of Hope’, and floats covered in flowers parade through the streets.
In summer and early autumn people swim in natural pools among black volcanic rocks, such as at Porto Moniz.
In December Funchal twinkles with countless lights, and the streets are full of music and festive treats.
On New Year’s Eve a giant fireworks show lights up Funchal Bay. In 2006 it entered the Guinness World Records.

tf.s: In Madeira you can ride down a hill in a big wicker basket on runners.
tf.w: These are the famous Monte sledges, steered by two drivers in straw hats.

tf.s: Cristiano Ronaldo was born in Madeira.
tf.w: He was born in Funchal, and the island’s airport is named after him.

tf.s: Madeira has long, snowy winters.
tf.w: Madeira is mild all year, so it is called the island of eternal spring.

tf.s: A long bridge joins Madeira to Lisbon.
tf.w: Madeira is an island far out in the ocean. People get there by plane or by ship.

azores.name: Azores
facts: The Azores are nine volcanic islands in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.
This is one of the best places in the world to see whales. Big sperm whales live around the islands all year.
At Sete Cidades two lakes lie side by side, one green and one blue. A legend says they came from the tears of a princess and a shepherd.
In Furnas a stew called cozido is cooked for hours in holes in the hot volcanic ground.
Pico, a volcano on the island of the same name, is the highest mountain in Portugal.
In summer blue hydrangeas grow along the roads like hedges. Faial is even called the blue island.

events.d: In spring blue whales, the biggest animals on Earth, swim past the islands, and boats go out to see them.
From spring into summer, villages hold festivals where everyone is offered soup and sweet bread.
In summer thousands of blue and lilac hydrangeas line the roads and fields.
At the end of summer the ocean is at its warmest, and people swim in natural pools among black lava rocks.
When the weather is cool, it is lovely to bathe in the warm springs of Furnas. The water is orange-brown from iron.

tf.s: In the Azores two lakes lie side by side, one green and one blue.
tf.w: They are the lakes of Sete Cidades, in the crater of an old volcano.

tf.s: Tea grows in the Azores.
tf.w: On São Miguel there are tea plantations, some of the oldest in Europe.

tf.s: The Azores are one big island.
tf.w: There are nine islands, scattered across the ocean.

tf.s: Penguins live on the beaches of the Azores.
tf.w: There are no penguins there, but whales, dolphins and sea turtles swim around the islands.

madrid.name: Madrid
facts: Madrid’s symbol is a bear reaching for the fruit of a strawberry tree. Its statue stands in the Puerta del Sol square.
In the same square a small plaque on the ground marks Kilometre Zero, the point from which Spain’s roads are measured.
The Royal Palace of Madrid has more than 3,000 rooms. It is one of the biggest palaces in Europe.
In Retiro Park you can row a boat on a big pond and visit a palace made of glass.
Try churros con chocolate: crispy fried dough sticks that you dip in thick hot chocolate.
In Spain a little mouse called Ratoncito Pérez collects children’s baby teeth. The story says he lives in Madrid, and his tiny house is a museum.

events.d: On the evening of 5 January the Three Kings ride through the streets throwing sweets, and on 6 January children find presents.
In mid-May people in Madrid wear checked caps and polka-dot dresses, dance the chotis and eat little doughnuts called rosquillas.
Summers in Madrid are hot and there is no sea, so families cool off in outdoor swimming pools.
On an autumn Sunday shepherds lead a huge flock of sheep through the centre of Madrid, along an ancient herding route.
From late November the Plaza Mayor fills with a Christmas market selling nativity figures, decorations and funny wigs.

tf.s: On New Year’s Eve people in Madrid eat 12 grapes as the clock strikes midnight.
tf.w: One grape for each chime of the clock in Puerta del Sol, for good luck in each of the 12 months.

tf.s: The oldest restaurant in the world is in Madrid.
tf.w: Restaurante Botín has been open since 1725, says the Guinness World Records.

tf.s: The symbol of Madrid is a lion eating an orange.
tf.w: It is a bear reaching for the fruit of a strawberry tree.

tf.s: The Royal Palace of Madrid has only 10 rooms.
tf.w: It has more than 3,000 rooms!

barcelona.name: Barcelona
facts: The Sagrada Família is a giant church designed by Antoni Gaudí. Builders started it in 1882 and are still working on it.
In Park Güell a big lizard covered in colourful broken tiles guards the steps. People also call it the dragon.
Casa Batlló is a house by Gaudí with wavy walls and a roof that looks like a dragon’s back.
Barcelona has sandy beaches right in the city: a museum in the morning, a swim in the sea in the afternoon!
People here speak two languages, Catalan and Spanish. ‘Thank you’ in Catalan is ‘gràcies’.
Try crema catalana, a creamy pudding with a crunchy top of burnt sugar that cracks under your spoon.

events.t: The Three Kings arrive by ship
events.d: On 5 January the Three Kings sail into Barcelona’s port, then parade through the city throwing sweets to children.
On 23 April the streets fill with stalls of books and roses, and people give each other a book or a rose.
In summer the Mediterranean is warm enough for swimming, building sandcastles and eating ice cream by the sea.
In late September the city celebrates: people build human towers on each other’s shoulders, and giant puppets dance in the streets.
Children ‘feed’ a smiling wooden log. At Christmas they tap it with sticks and sing, and it ‘gives’ them sweets.

tf.s: Builders have been working on the Sagrada Família for more than 140 years.
tf.w: Work began in 1882, and the church is still being finished.

tf.s: At festivals in Barcelona people build towers out of people.
tf.w: They are called castells: people stand on each other’s shoulders, and a child climbs to the very top.

tf.s: Gaudí’s lizard in Park Güell is made of gold.
tf.w: It is covered with pieces of colourful broken tiles.

tf.s: Barcelona is the capital of Spain.
tf.w: The capital of Spain is Madrid. Barcelona is the second biggest city in Spain.

seville.name: Seville
facts: Seville is one of the homes of flamenco, a dance with stamping feet, clapping hands and guitar music. There is even a flamenco museum.
Instead of stairs, the Giralda tower has 35 ramps. They are so wide that people could ride up to the top on horseback.
Seville Cathedral is the biggest Gothic cathedral in the world. The tomb of Christopher Columbus is inside.
Thousands of orange trees grow along the streets. Their oranges are bitter, and many are sent to Britain to make marmalade.
At Plaza de España you can row a little boat along a canal, past benches made of colourful painted tiles.
Las Setas, ‘the mushrooms’, is a giant wooden roof over the old town. You can walk along the top of it.

events.d: In December a market sells figures for nativity scenes, and churches and shops show whole miniature villages.
In winter the street trees are full of orange fruit, and in January and February it is picked.
In spring the orange trees are covered in white blossom, and the whole city smells sweet.
For a whole week people dance sevillanas in frilly dresses, ride in horse carriages and go on fairground rides.
In summer Seville is one of the hottest cities in Europe. People rest in the shade by day and go out in the cool evening.

tf.s: Peacocks walk in the gardens of the Alcázar palace in Seville.
tf.w: They stroll among the fountains and orange trees of the old royal gardens.

tf.s: Scenes of a Star Wars film were shot in Seville.
tf.w: In the film, Plaza de España became part of the planet Naboo.

tf.s: The oranges on Seville’s street trees are very sweet.
tf.w: They are bitter, so they are used for marmalade, not eaten straight from the tree.

tf.s: Seville stands on the seashore.
tf.w: Seville is on the river Guadalquivir, and ships can still sail up it from the sea.

tenerife.name: Tenerife
facts: Teide, a volcano on Tenerife, is the highest mountain in Spain. A cable car carries people high up its slopes.
Many beaches here have black sand made from volcanic rock. The golden sand of Las Teresitas beach was brought from the Sahara Desert.
Pilot whales and dolphins live in the sea near Tenerife all year, and boats take people out to watch them.
In the town of Icod de los Vinos grows a very old dragon tree. When its bark is cut, the sap turns red.
Try papas arrugadas: little wrinkly potatoes boiled in very salty water and eaten with red or green mojo sauce.
Canary birds are named after the Canary Islands, not the other way round. The islands’ name probably comes from the Latin word for dogs.

events.d: In winter Teide’s peak is often white with snow, while down on the beaches it is warm and sunny.
One of the biggest carnivals in the world, with parades, music and a carnival queen in a huge sparkling costume.
For Corpus Christi, the town of La Orotava covers its main square with huge pictures made of coloured sand from Teide.
From late summer into autumn the ocean around Tenerife is at its warmest, the best time for swimming and snorkelling.
In late November children in Puerto de la Cruz drag strings of rattling tin cans through the streets. The louder, the better!

tf.s: The highest mountain in Spain is a volcano on Tenerife.
tf.w: It is Teide, more than 3,700 metres high.

tf.s: The sand of one beach on Tenerife came from the Sahara Desert.
tf.w: The golden sand of Las Teresitas beach was brought from the Sahara by ship.

tf.s: The Canary Islands are named after canary birds.
tf.w: It is the other way round: the birds are named after the islands.

tf.s: Teide is covered in snow all year round.
tf.w: Snow falls on Teide mostly in winter. In summer its top is bare.

mallorca.name: Mallorca
facts: Mallorca is the biggest of the Balearic Islands in the Mediterranean Sea.
In the Caves of Drach there is a huge underground lake. Musicians play a concert in boats floating on the water.
Since 1912 an old wooden train has run from Palma through the mountains to Sóller. From there an old tram takes you to the sea.
Try an ensaïmada, a soft spiral pastry dusted with icing sugar. People carry them home on the plane in big boxes.
Palma Cathedral stands right by the sea. Its huge round window is called the Gothic Eye.
The water here is very clear thanks to underwater meadows of a sea plant called Posidonia.

events.d: On 17 January, St Anthony’s Day, people bring their dogs, cats, horses and even hens to be blessed.
In late winter thousands of almond trees burst into white and pink flowers, and the fields look snowy.
In spring the Tramuntana mountains are green and full of wild flowers, a perfect time for family walks.
On 2 February and 11 November the morning sun shines through the big round window of Palma Cathedral. It paints a bright ‘8’ on the wall.
From June to October the sea is warm, and the water in the coves is so clear you can see the fish.

tf.s: In Mallorca you can listen to music played in boats on an underground lake.
tf.w: It happens in the Caves of Drach, on a lake deep inside the rock.

tf.s: The tennis star Rafael Nadal was born in Mallorca.
tf.w: He was born in the town of Manacor, where he now has a tennis academy.

tf.s: Mallorca is in the Atlantic Ocean.
tf.w: Mallorca is an island in the Mediterranean Sea.

tf.s: An ensaïmada is a salty fish pie.
tf.w: It is a sweet spiral pastry dusted with icing sugar.

paris.name: Paris
facts: The Eiffel Tower was built for a world fair in 1889. In the evening it sparkles with thousands of lights for a few minutes every hour.
The Louvre is one of the biggest art museums in the world. It has a glass pyramid at the entrance and the famous Mona Lisa inside.
In the Luxembourg Gardens children push little wooden sailing boats across a big pond with sticks.
The Ménagerie in the Jardin des Plantes is one of the oldest zoos in the world. It opened more than 200 years ago.
On the hill of Montmartre artists paint pictures right in the square, and a white church looks down over the city.
French bakers make fresh baguettes every day. In 2022 the craft of the baguette was added to UNESCO’s list of world traditions.

events.d: In January families share a galette des rois with a tiny figure hidden inside. Whoever finds it wears a paper crown.
On 2 February the French make crêpes. For luck, you flip one in the pan while holding a coin in your other hand.
On 21 June, at the start of summer, musicians play in streets, squares and parks, and everyone can listen for free.
In summer sand and deckchairs appear along the Seine, and on 14 July fireworks sparkle around the Eiffel Tower.
From late November the Champs-Élysées glow with lights, and the windows of big department stores fill with moving toys.

tf.s: The Paris metro opened more than 120 years ago.
tf.w: The first line opened in 1900.

tf.s: The Eiffel Tower is repainted about every seven years.
tf.w: Painters do it by hand with brushes and use about 60 tonnes of paint.

tf.s: The Eiffel Tower is made of wood.
tf.w: It is made of iron: more than 18,000 metal parts held together by millions of rivets.

tf.s: The Mona Lisa is a giant painting as big as a wall.
tf.w: It is quite small, only about 77 by 53 centimetres.

nice.name: Nice
facts: The Promenade des Anglais runs along the Bay of Angels. Its name means ‘the walk of the English’, because English visitors helped build it about 200 years ago.
The beaches of Nice are covered with round, smooth pebbles instead of sand, so water shoes are handy.
Blue chairs stand along the seafront. They are a symbol of the city, and anyone can sit on them and watch the sea.
Try socca, a thin, crispy pancake made from chickpea flour and baked in a big pan in a very hot oven.
The Cours Saleya market in the old town is full of flowers, fruit and vegetables.
Castle Hill has no castle any more, but it has a park, a waterfall and a view over the whole bay.

events.d: In winter the hills around Nice turn yellow with fluffy mimosa flowers.

events.t: Carnival and the Battle of Flowers
events.d: At the carnival giant figures roll through the streets. In the Battle of Flowers, people on decorated floats throw flowers to the crowd.
In nearby Menton, giant sculptures are made from tonnes of lemons and oranges.
In summer the Mediterranean at Nice is warm and clear, perfect for swimming and looking at fish with a mask.
In December a Christmas village with lights and an ice rink opens in the centre of Nice.

tf.s: The beaches of Nice are covered with pebbles, not sand.
tf.w: The round stones are smooth, and they rattle when the waves roll them.

tf.s: The artist Henri Matisse lived in Nice, and there is a museum of his work there.
tf.w: The Matisse Museum stands on the hill of Cimiez, among olive trees.

tf.s: Socca is a chocolate pancake.
tf.w: Socca is made from chickpea flour, with no chocolate at all.

tf.s: Nice is on the coast of the Atlantic Ocean.
tf.w: Nice is on the Mediterranean Sea, on the French Riviera.

rome.name: Rome
facts: The Colosseum is a giant stone arena almost 2,000 years old. Tens of thousands of people could sit inside to watch the shows.
Throw a coin over your shoulder into the Trevi Fountain, and legend says you will come back to Rome. The coins are collected to help people in need.
The Pantheon has a huge dome with a round hole at the top. When it rains, raindrops fall inside and drain away through little holes in the floor.
Many cats live among ancient ruins at Largo di Torre Argentina, where volunteers look after them.
Rome has about 2,500 street fountains called nasoni. Block the spout with your finger, and water shoots up from a little hole for drinking.
Try supplì, a fried rice ball with mozzarella inside. When you bite it, the cheese stretches like a telephone cord.

events.d: A giant Christmas tree and a nativity scene stand in St Peter’s Square. On 6 January the kind old Befana brings children sweets.
At Carnival children wear costumes, throw colourful confetti and eat frappe, crispy fried pastry with icing sugar.
On 21 April Rome celebrates its birthday, and people dressed as ancient Romans parade through the old streets.
Summers in Rome are hot, so families take the train to the beaches of Ostia for a swim.
On 5 August white petals fall from the ceiling of the church of Santa Maria Maggiore. They recall a legend about summer snow.

tf.s: The smallest country in the world is inside Rome.
tf.w: It is Vatican City. You can simply walk into it across a square.

tf.s: Rome has a stone face that, legend says, bites the hand of anyone who tells a lie.
tf.w: It is the Mouth of Truth. Visitors put a hand in its mouth for a photo, but it is only a legend!

tf.s: The Colosseum was built about 100 years ago.
tf.w: It is almost 2,000 years old: it was finished in the year 80.

tf.s: You have to pay for water from Rome’s street fountains.
tf.w: Water from the nasoni fountains is free, fresh and good to drink.

venice.name: Venice
facts: Venice stands on more than 100 small islands in a lagoon, joined together by about 400 bridges.
There are no cars in Venice. Buses are boats called vaporetti, and even ambulances and taxis float!
Gondolas are long black boats. The gondolier stands at the back and rows with just one oar.
The Grand Canal winds through the city like a giant snake. Cross it on the old Rialto Bridge, which has shops on it.
The symbol of Venice is a lion with wings. Look for him on walls, flags and columns!
At carnival time, Venetians fry frìtole: sweet doughnut balls with raisins, dusted with sugar.

events.d: People in beautiful masks and costumes stroll through the squares, like in a fairy tale.
Thousands of boats, from gondolas to kayaks and dragon boats, row about 30 kilometres round the lagoon just for fun.
The sea is warm at the Lido beach, and in July huge Redentore fireworks light up the lagoon.
Boats decorated as in olden times parade along the Grand Canal, and then rowers race each other.
Christmas lights sparkle, and on 6 January rowers dressed as the Befana, a kind old witch, race on the Grand Canal.

tf.s: In Venice, even ambulances are boats.
tf.w: Ambulances, taxis and buses all travel on the water in Venice.

tf.s: On the island of Burano, the houses are painted in bright colours.
tf.w: Burano's houses are pink, blue, yellow and green, like a box of crayons.

tf.s: Gondoliers row with two oars, one in each hand.
tf.w: A gondolier uses just one long oar and rows standing up.

tf.s: Venice has an underground train, just like London.
tf.w: Venice has no metro and no cars: people walk or take water buses.

florence.name: Florence
facts: The cathedral has a giant red dome, finished almost 600 years ago. You can climb 463 steps to the top!
Michelangelo carved the statue of David from one block of marble. David is more than 5 metres tall!
The Ponte Vecchio is an old bridge with shops built right on it. They sell gold and jewellery.
Rub the nose of the bronze boar, Il Porcellino, for luck. That is why it shines so brightly!
Carlo Collodi, the writer who invented Pinocchio, was born in Florence.
Try schiacciata, a soft, flat Tuscan bread with olive oil and salt.

events.d: Children in costumes throw confetti, and bakeries sell a soft orange cake decorated with the city's lily.
On Easter morning, a dove-shaped rocket whizzes out of the cathedral and lights fireworks on a huge old cart.
On 24 June, St John's Day, fireworks sparkle over the river Arno, and all summer gelato helps you cool down.
On the evening of 7 September, children walk through the streets with colourful paper lanterns on long sticks.
A tall Christmas tree shines in the cathedral square, and on 6 January the Befana fills children's stockings with sweets.

tf.s: Florence's flag shows a red flower on a white background.
tf.w: It is a red lily, and its shape comes from the iris flower.

tf.s: A bronze copy of David stands on a square where you can see the whole city.
tf.w: It is Piazzale Michelangelo, on a hill with a view of the red roofs and the cathedral dome.

tf.s: Michelangelo's David is as small as a doll.
tf.w: The real David is more than 5 metres tall, taller than three grown-ups standing on each other.

tf.s: In Florence, people rub the nose of a bronze cat for luck.
tf.w: It is a bronze boar called Il Porcellino, the 'little pig'.

london.name: London
facts: Big Ben is not the clock tower itself: it is the name of the huge bell inside it.
London's famous buses are red and have two floors. Sit upstairs at the front for the best view!
The London Underground, called the Tube, opened in 1863. It is the oldest underground railway in the world.
Ravens live at the Tower of London, and a special guard called the Ravenmaster looks after them.
Pelicans live in St James's Park! The first ones were a gift from a Russian ambassador more than 350 years ago.
Try fish and chips, or scones with jam and cream at teatime.

events.d: Dragon and lion dancers, drums and red lanterns fill Chinatown and Trafalgar Square.
Daffodils fill the parks, and in April thousands of runners, some dressed as dinosaurs, race in the London Marathon.

events.t: Summer: the King's parade and tennis
events.d: In June guards parade for the King's birthday, and in July tennis fans eat strawberries and cream at Wimbledon.
Steel drums, feathers and dancing fill the streets, and Sunday is the special day for children and families.
Hyde Park turns into a winter fair with an ice rink, rides and a Christmas market.

tf.s: A blue whale skeleton hangs from the ceiling of the Natural History Museum.
tf.w: The whale is called Hope, and it is more than 25 metres long.

tf.s: One trip round on the London Eye wheel takes about half an hour.
tf.w: One turn takes about 30 minutes, and from the top you can see far across the city.

tf.s: The King's guards at Buckingham Palace wear tall white fluffy hats.
tf.w: Their tall fluffy hats, called bearskins, are black.

tf.s: Big Ben is the tallest building in London.
tf.w: Big Ben is a bell in a clock tower. The tallest building in London is the Shard.

amsterdam.name: Amsterdam
facts: Amsterdam has more than 100 kilometres of canals and about 1,500 bridges.
People ride bikes everywhere. Parents often carry their children in a big box at the front of the bike!
Look up at the tall, narrow houses: many have a hook at the top for lifting furniture in through the windows.
The Royal Palace stands on 13,659 wooden poles pushed deep into the wet ground.
Dutch children love bread with hagelslag, chocolate sprinkles, for breakfast. Try poffertjes too: tiny fluffy pancakes!
One houseboat on a canal is a home for cats. It is called the Poezenboot, the Cat Boat.

events.d: Tulips bloom in the parks and in huge striped fields outside the city: red, yellow and purple.
On 27 April everyone wears orange, and children sell their old toys at a giant street market.

events.t: Summer in the parks and by the sea
events.d: Families picnic in the Vondelpark, and the sandy beach at Zandvoort is about half an hour away by train.
In November Sinterklaas arrives by boat, and on 5 December children get presents and chocolate letters.
On dark winter evenings, glowing artworks shine along the canals, and you can see them from a boat.

tf.s: Amsterdam's Artis Zoo is almost 200 years old.
tf.w: Artis opened in 1838. It is the oldest zoo in the Netherlands.

tf.s: Some people in Amsterdam live in houseboats on the canals.
tf.w: There are about 2,500 houseboats on Amsterdam's canals.

tf.s: The famous painting The Night Watch is the size of a postcard.
tf.w: Rembrandt's painting in the Rijksmuseum is huge: almost 4 metres high and about 4.5 metres wide.

tf.s: In Amsterdam, people may ride bikes only on Sundays.
tf.w: People ride bikes every day: to school, to work and to the shops.

berlin.name: Berlin
facts: The bear is the symbol of Berlin. Look for big, colourful bear statues around the city, called Buddy Bears.
On top of the Brandenburg Gate stands a chariot pulled by four horses.
The TV Tower is 368 metres tall, the tallest structure in Germany. In the ball at the top, a restaurant slowly turns round.
Berlin Zoo opened in 1844. It is the oldest zoo in Germany that is still open.
On many traffic lights, a little green man in a hat tells you when to cross. He is called the Ampelmann.
Try currywurst: a sausage with ketchup and curry powder. It was first sold in Berlin in 1949.

events.d: Children hunt for eggs hidden by the Easter Bunny, and markets sell painted eggs and chocolate bunnies.
Families swim and build sandcastles at lakes like the Wannsee, which has a long sandy beach.
Runners and inline skaters race through the city, and many world records have been set here.
For ten evenings, famous buildings are covered in bright moving pictures made of light.
Markets sell gingerbread and hot apple punch, and on 31 December fireworks light up the Brandenburg Gate.

tf.s: Berlin's natural history museum has one of the tallest dinosaur skeletons in the world.
tf.w: The giant Giraffatitan skeleton there is more than 13 metres tall.

tf.s: In Berlin, jam doughnuts are called Pfannkuchen, which means pancakes.
tf.w: Berliners call them Pfannkuchen, while in many other parts of Germany they are called Berliners!

tf.s: A dragon statue stands on top of the Brandenburg Gate.
tf.w: On top there is a chariot pulled by four horses.

tf.s: The little man on Berlin's traffic lights wears a crown.
tf.w: He wears a hat, and he is called the Ampelmann.

munich.name: Munich
facts: Every day at 11 and 12 o'clock, figures dance in the Glockenspiel on the town hall tower. At the end, a tiny golden bird chirps!
The English Garden is one of the biggest city parks in the world, even larger than Central Park in New York.
The Deutsches Museum is one of the biggest science museums in the world, with real planes and ships.
Try a soft pretzel, called a Brezn. By tradition, people in Munich eat white sausages with sweet mustard before noon!
On a clear day, you can see the snowy Alps from Munich.
Hellabrunn Zoo was the first zoo in the world where animals are grouped by the continent they come from.

events.d: Children dress up in costumes, and on the last day the market women dance at the Viktualienmarkt.
It is the little sister of Oktoberfest, with merry-go-rounds, rides and gingerbread hearts.
On hot days, families paddle and picnic on the pebbly banks of the river Isar.
The world's biggest folk festival has a Ferris wheel, roller coasters and people in traditional clothes.
Wooden stalls on Marienplatz sell toys, roasted almonds and gingerbread next to a giant Christmas tree.

tf.s: The symbol of Munich is a child dressed as a monk.
tf.w: He is called the Münchner Kindl, and the name Munich comes from the word for monks.

tf.s: Oktoberfest starts in September.
tf.w: The festival starts in September and ends in early October.

tf.s: The Glockenspiel figures on Marienplatz dance only once a year.
tf.w: They dance every day at 11 and 12 o'clock.

tf.s: Munich is by the sea.
tf.w: Munich is far from the sea, but close to the Alps mountains.

vienna.name: Vienna
facts: The giant Ferris wheel in the Prater park was built in 1897. Its red cabins look like little houses.
Schönbrunn Palace, where emperors spent their summers, has 1,441 rooms and a maze in its garden.
At the Spanish Riding School, white Lipizzaner horses dance to music. The foals are born dark and turn white as they grow.
Try Sachertorte, a chocolate cake with apricot jam, first made in Vienna in 1832.
Vienna is a city of music. Mozart lived here, and a golden statue of Johann Strauss plays the violin in the city park.
The river Danube flows through Vienna. A long island in the middle of the river is perfect for swimming and cycling.

events.d: On 1 January, the orchestra plays waltzes, and the audience claps along to the last march.

events.t: Ice skating at the City Hall
events.d: The square in front of the City Hall becomes a big ice rink, with skating paths winding through the park.
Markets at Schönbrunn Palace and in the old town sell beautifully painted eggs.
People swim, cycle and have picnics, and in early summer a huge free music festival takes place there.
Trees by the City Hall sparkle with lights, and stalls sell toys, gingerbread and warm children's punch.

tf.s: Vienna has the oldest zoo in the world that is still open.
tf.w: Schönbrunn Zoo opened in 1752, more than 270 years ago.

tf.s: The Vienna Boys' Choir is more than 500 years old.
tf.w: It was founded in 1498, and the boys still sing in sailor suits.

tf.s: Mozart was born in Vienna.
tf.w: Mozart was born in Salzburg, but he lived in Vienna and wrote much of his music here.

tf.s: The roof of St Stephen's Cathedral is made of gold.
tf.w: It is covered with about 230,000 colourful tiles that make zigzag patterns.

prague.name: Prague
facts: Prague Castle is one of the largest castle complexes in the world. Watch the guards change at noon!
The Astronomical Clock is more than 600 years old. Every hour, little figures appear in its windows and a golden rooster crows.
The old stone Charles Bridge has 30 statues along its sides, and musicians and artists work on it.
Prague has puppet theatres and shops full of marionettes. Czech puppetry is on UNESCO's list of world treasures.
Swans glide on the Vltava river, and people come to the riverbank to watch them.
Smell the trdelník: sweet dough wrapped round a stick, baked over a fire and rolled in sugar.

events.d: The Old Town Square fills with stalls selling painted eggs, wooden toys and gingerbread.
From spring to autumn you can rent a pedal boat and paddle along the Vltava among the swans.
For a few autumn evenings, light shows and glowing artworks turn the old streets into a magical world.
On 5 December, St Nicholas, an angel and a cheeky devil give sweets to children who say a poem.
A tall Christmas tree shines on the Old Town Square, surrounded by stalls with treats and toys.

tf.s: The cartoon Little Mole was created by a Czech artist.
tf.w: Zdeněk Miler drew the Little Mole, Krtek, and you can find him in many toy shops in Prague.

tf.s: Inside Prague Castle there is a lane of tiny colourful houses.
tf.w: It is called Golden Lane, and some doors are so low that grown-ups have to bend down.

tf.s: The tower on Petřín Hill is taller than the Eiffel Tower.
tf.w: It looks like a little Eiffel Tower, but it is only about 60 metres tall.

tf.s: The Astronomical Clock was built just 50 years ago.
tf.w: It is more than 600 years old and still works.

athens.name: Athens
facts: On the Acropolis hill stands the Parthenon, a temple built for the goddess Athena about 2,500 years ago.
Legend says Athena gave the city an olive tree, so the people named Athens after her.
The guards called Evzones wear pleated skirts and shoes with big pompoms, and they march with slow, high steps.
The owl was Athena's bird. Look at a Greek one-euro coin: it shows an owl from an ancient Athenian coin!
The Panathenaic Stadium is made all of white marble. The first modern Olympic Games were held there in 1896.
Try souvlaki, little pieces of meat grilled on a stick, and thick Greek yoghurt with honey.

events.d: On this spring holiday, families picnic on the hills and fill the sky with colourful kites.
Children dye eggs red and tap them together: the one whose egg doesn't crack wins.

events.t: Summer: the sea and open-air cinema
events.d: The sea near Athens is warm for swimming, and in the evening you can watch films outdoors under the stars.
Runners follow the route of the first Olympic marathon and finish in the marble stadium.
Children sing carols with little triangles, and on New Year's Day a cake hides a lucky coin.

tf.s: In the Acropolis Museum, you can walk on glass floors above ancient streets.
tf.w: Through the glass floor you can see the remains of an old neighbourhood right under your feet.

tf.s: The first modern Olympic Games took place in Athens.
tf.w: They were held in 1896, in the marble Panathenaic Stadium.

tf.s: The Parthenon was built about 200 years ago.
tf.w: It is much older: about 2,500 years old.

tf.s: Athens was named after the sea god Poseidon.
tf.w: It is named after the goddess Athena, who, the legend says, gave the city an olive tree.

crete.name: Crete
facts: Crete is the biggest Greek island. It has high mountains, deep gorges and hundreds of beaches.
The palace of Knossos is almost 4,000 years old. Legends say a great maze, the Labyrinth, was here.
The kri-kri is a wild goat with long curved horns. It lives in the wild only on Crete and a few tiny islands nearby.
Greek myths say that baby Zeus, king of the gods, was hidden in a cave on Crete.
One olive tree in the village of Vouves is more than 2,000 years old, and it still grows olives!
At Elafonisi beach the sand is pink, coloured by tiny pieces of shells.

events.d: The town of Rethymno holds the biggest carnival on Crete, with costumes, music and a big parade.
The hills are covered with wild flowers, and families dye eggs red for Easter.
From June to October the sea is warm and clear, perfect for swimming and snorkelling among little fish.
Loggerhead sea turtles lay eggs in the sand at night, and later the tiny babies crawl to the sea.
Families spread big nets under the trees and shake the branches so the olives fall down.

tf.s: Sea turtles lay their eggs on some beaches of Crete.
tf.w: Loggerhead turtles nest on beaches such as those near Rethymno and Chania.

tf.s: Crete has a gorge so long that walking through it takes most of a day.
tf.w: The Samaria Gorge is about 16 kilometres long, and walkers need 5 to 7 hours.

tf.s: Crete is the smallest Greek island.
tf.w: Crete is the biggest Greek island.

tf.s: The kri-kri is a little bird that sings 'kri-kri'.
tf.w: The kri-kri is a wild goat with long curved horns.

istanbul.name: Istanbul
facts: Istanbul stands on two continents, Europe and Asia. A ferry can take you from one to the other in less than half an hour.
Thousands of street cats live in Istanbul. People feed them and even build little houses for them.
The Grand Bazaar is one of the oldest and biggest covered markets in the world, with about 4,000 shops.
The Blue Mosque has six tall towers called minarets, and inside it is decorated with more than 20,000 tiles.
Try simit: a ring of bread covered in sesame seeds, sold from little red carts.
Turkish ice cream, dondurma, is so stretchy that sellers play tricks with it before they hand you the cone!

events.d: Millions of tulips bloom in the parks, and some flower beds look like giant colourful carpets.
On 5 and 6 May, people welcome spring and tie wishes written on paper to rose bushes.
A ferry takes you to islands with almost no cars, where you can ride bikes and swim in the sea.
Runners start in Asia, cross a big bridge over the Bosphorus and finish in Europe.
Street sellers roast chestnuts, and cafés serve salep, a hot milky drink with cinnamon.

tf.s: Under Istanbul there is an ancient underground water tank with 336 columns.
tf.w: The Basilica Cistern once stored water for the city, and today fish swim in it.

tf.s: Tulips were loved in Istanbul before they became famous in the Netherlands.
tf.w: Tulips travelled to Western Europe from the Ottoman lands more than 400 years ago.

tf.s: Istanbul is entirely in Europe.
tf.w: Istanbul is on two continents: part of it is in Europe and part is in Asia.

tf.s: Simit is a chocolate cake.
tf.w: Simit is a ring of bread covered in sesame seeds.

spb.name: Saint Petersburg
facts: Peter the Great founded the city in 1703 on islands where the river Neva meets the sea. With so many canals, it is called the Venice of the North.
At night, the big bridges over the Neva open up to let ships sail through.
In June it never gets really dark at night. These light nights are called the White Nights.
The Hermitage is one of the biggest museums in the world. Cats live in its cellars and help keep the mice away!
At Peterhof palace there are more than 150 fountains. Some are jokes that splash you if you step on the wrong stone!
Try pyshki: hot doughnuts dusted with powdered sugar, a favourite treat in the city.

events.d: People say goodbye to winter with games, sledging and piles of hot bliny, thin pancakes.
From spring to autumn, golden statues and fountains sparkle in the palace park by the sea.
In late June, a ship with bright red sails glides along the Neva, and fireworks sparkle in the light night sky.
In Pavlovsk Park, among the yellow leaves, tame squirrels take nuts right from your hand.
A big New Year tree shines on Palace Square, and Ded Moroz, Grandfather Frost, brings presents.

tf.s: On the Fontanka river there is a tiny bird statue, and people try to land a coin on it for luck.
tf.w: It is called Chizhik-Pyzhik, one of the smallest statues in the city.

tf.s: Saint Petersburg has more than 300 bridges.
tf.w: More than 300 bridges cross its rivers and canals.

tf.s: The bridges over the Neva open in the middle of the day.
tf.w: They open at night, when the streets are quiet, so that ships can pass.

tf.s: Pyshki are little fish pies.
tf.w: Pyshki are hot doughnuts dusted with powdered sugar.

moscow.name: Moscow
facts: St Basil's Cathedral on Red Square has colourful domes with stripes and swirls, like giant sweets.
The Tsar Bell in the Kremlin is the biggest bell in the world. It weighs over 200 tonnes but has never rung!
Many metro stations look like underground palaces, with chandeliers, mosaics and marble.
The Ostankino TV Tower is 540 metres tall, the tallest tower in Europe.
On the Puppet Theatre there is a clock with 12 little houses for fairy-tale animals. At noon all the doors open and the animals come out!
Try bliny, thin Russian pancakes, with sour cream, jam or honey.

events.d: Parks hold fairs with games, music and stacks of bliny to say goodbye to winter.
The old apple orchards of Kolomenskoye park turn white and pink with blossom.
River boats sail past the Kremlin, and the parks have fountains, rowing boats and bike paths.
In early September, Moscow celebrates its birthday with concerts, street shows and fireworks.
Ded Moroz and his granddaughter Snegurochka visit children, and squares turn into ice rinks.

tf.s: Giant pandas live in Moscow Zoo.
tf.w: Pandas came from China in 2019, and a baby panda was born there in 2023.

tf.s: The ballet Swan Lake was first performed in Moscow.
tf.w: It was first shown at the Bolshoi Theatre in 1877, with music by Tchaikovsky.

tf.s: The Tsar Bell rings every morning.
tf.w: It has never rung: a big piece broke off before it could be hung.

tf.s: All the domes of St Basil's Cathedral are plain white.
tf.w: Its domes are bright and colourful, with stripes and swirls.

newyork.name: New York
facts: The Statue of Liberty was a gift from France. Her index finger is about 2.4 metres long, longer than a grown-up is tall!
Central Park is a giant park in the middle of Manhattan. It has a zoo, a carousel and an Alice in Wonderland statue to climb on.
The Empire State Building has 102 floors, and its top lights up in different colours for holidays.
Yellow taxis are everywhere, and the subway runs all day and all night.
At the Museum of Natural History, a life-size blue whale model as long as a basketball court hangs from the ceiling.
Try a giant slice of New York pizza, a bagel or a hot dog from a street cart.

events.d: Pink cherry trees bloom in Central Park and in the Brooklyn Botanic Garden.
Families swim at the beach, ride the old Wonder Wheel, and on 4 July watch huge fireworks.
Children dress up in costumes and go from door to door saying 'Trick or treat!' to get sweets.
Giant balloons of cartoon characters, taller than houses, float through the streets of Manhattan.
A giant Christmas tree glows above an ice rink, and shop windows turn into fairy-tale scenes.

tf.s: Coney Island's Wonder Wheel is more than 100 years old.
tf.w: It opened in 1920 and still gives rides today.

tf.s: The Brooklyn Bridge opened more than 140 years ago.
tf.w: It opened in 1883, and you can walk across it on a wooden path above the cars.

tf.s: The Statue of Liberty has always been green.
tf.w: At first she was shiny copper-brown, and she slowly turned green over many years.

tf.s: New York taxis are famous for being red.
tf.w: New York's famous taxis are yellow.

items.m: Thank you! (a boy says / a girl says)
